sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Yùhuáng** (*yuhuang*) — Jade Emperor, Heaven, Sovereignty · Jade Emperor — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Jade Emperor, Heaven, Sovereignty". The name means "Jade Emperor"[^1].

**Yùhuáng** belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is associated with jade emperor, heaven, sovereignty.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Yùhuáng** and serves its temple at [yuhuang.com](https://punicodex.com/yuhuang/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *yuhuang* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^2].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Chinese characters as **玉皇**. Etymologically it means "Jade Emperor"[^1].

Yù (玉) 'jade'; Huáng (皇) 'emperor, sovereign' — the supreme deity of Chinese folk religion and Taoist cosmology.

The ASCII form *yuhuang* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Yùhuáng** recovers the stress accent of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **y** → **Y** — Same, capitalized
- **u** → **ù** — Grave tone mark
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **u** → **u** — Same
- **a** → **á** — Acute tone mark
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **g** → **g** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is served at **yuhuang.com**[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/yuhuang/** — Chinese Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Y** — Initial character of the restored form Yùhuáng.
- **ùhuáng** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Chinese tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'YUHUANG' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — Yùhuáng, the restored Unicode form of the name

Yùhuáng is Tier 1 because the Chinese form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The stories of **Yùhuáng** circulate within the Chinese corpus, where the figure embodies jade emperor, heaven, sovereignty.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Yùhuáng is attested in the canonical Chinese sources as a figure associated with jade emperor, heaven, sovereignty.[^1]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "Jade Emperor" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Yùhuáng**, the Jade Emperor, is the supreme ruler of the Daoist celestial bureaucracy. He presides over the Three Realms—heaven, earth, and the underworld—and judges the dead at the Chinese New Year.[^1] His authority is administrative rather than creative; he delegates cosmic functions to a vast pantheon of ministers and generals. His birthday, celebrated on the ninth day of the first lunar month, involves offerings of incense, paper money, and vegetarian food across Chinese communities.[^1]

sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Yùhuáng appears within the Chinese tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[caishen|Cáishén]], [[change|Cháng'é]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guandi|Guāndì]], and [[guanyin|Guānyīn]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Yùhuáng continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Chinese tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] The Jade Emperor is honored throughout the Chinese-speaking world during New Year rituals and in temple cults that blend Daoist, Buddhist, and folk elements.[^1]

sections.label: Classical Texts
sections.body:
The figure of Yùhuáng descends from the high god **Shàngdì** of the **Shūjīng** and **Shījīng**, where he presides over harvest, warfare, and dynastic legitimacy.[^1] The **Shǐjì** records the First Emperor's sacrifices to heaven, and Han texts begin to identify Shàngdì with the impersonal **Tiān**.[^2]

Yùhuáng is thus the late-imperial personification of a cosmic sovereignty already present in Zhou classics.

sources.citation: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Daoist Sources
sections.body:
The **Dàozàng** contains scores of scriptures in which the Jade Emperor reveals cosmic law, judges souls, and delegates authority to celestial bureaux.[^1] The **Yùhuáng Jīng** and related liturgies place him at the summit of the Daoist pantheon, above the Three Pure Ones in popular practice.[^2]

Taoist ritual commonly opens with an invocation of the Jade Emperor as the supreme administrator of heaven.
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Buddhist Sources
sections.body:
Yùhuáng absorbed Buddhist models of cosmic kingship: like **Śakra/Indra**, he presides over a celestial bureaucracy, and like a **Dharma-protecting deity**, he supports the transmission of sutras.[^1] Chinese apocryphal texts and temple iconography often show him receiving Buddhist bodhisattvas.[^2]

The result is a distinctly Chinese supreme deity who rules both Daoist heavens and the Buddhist-inflected underworld.

sections.label: Calligraphy & Script
sections.body:
The characters **玉皇** (Jade Emperor) appear on temple plaques in solemn **kǎishū**, often gilded and framed by dragons.[^1] In Daoist talismans the same graphs are written in seal-script variants that identify the deity as a recipient of petitions and burnt offerings.[^2]

The tonal restoration **Yùhuáng** preserves the fourth-tone majesty and second-tone brightness of the imperial title.

sections.body: Yùhuáng embodies jade emperor, heaven, sovereignty in the Chinese imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]
